ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a square ABCD, with A at the upper left, B at the upper right, C at the lower right, and D at the lower left. Inside the square, four semicircular arcs with the vertices as centers intersect, and line segment PQ is horizontal; P is located on the left side and is the intersection point of the two arcs with B and C as centers, and Q is located on the right side and is the intersection point of the two arcs with A and D as centers. Reasoning: Let the side length of the square be 1, and take coordinates D=(0,0), C=(1,0), B=(1,1), A=(0,1). Because P is on the circles with B and C as centers and radius 1, it satisfies (x-1)^2+(y-1)^2=1 and (x-1)^2+y^2=1. Subtracting the two equations gives y=1/2. Substituting into (x-1)^2+y^2=1 gives (x-1)^2+1/4=1, so (x-1)^2=3/4. P is the left-side intersection point, therefore x=1-sqrt(3)/2. Similarly, Q is on the circles with A and D as centers and radius 1, satisfying x^2+(y-1)^2=1 and x^2+y^2=1. Subtracting gives y=1/2, and substituting again gives x^2+1/4=1, so x=sqrt(3)/2. Q is the right-side intersection point, therefore x=sqrt(3)/2. PQ is horizontal, so the length of PQ equals the difference of the x-coordinates: sqrt(3)/2 - (1 - sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3)-1.
